title: Mask-free interference lithography for every periodic array layer
idea: First principle: a DRAM array is a lattice whose whole information content is one unit cell plus two lattice vectors (~100 bits), yet each array layer goes through a $300k+ EUV mask and a ~$200M projection scanner. Print the active, wordline, bitline and storage-node-contact layers with a reticle-free 4-beam 193i (or EUV) interference stepper that has no projection optics, and trim the array edges with one coarse DUV block mask, so masks are needed only for the periphery.
why: Litho capital and masks (fact 4): an interference tool costs ~1/5-1/10 as much as a scanner per wafer-pass and removes 3-5 EUV array exposures; claimed ~20-30% lower wafer cost.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina pores as capacitor molds
idea: First principle: high-AR plasma etch fights ion angular spread and neutral transport, but anodic Al2O3 pores grow by field-assisted dissolution at a pitch set by voltage (~2.5 nm/V) and keep going to any depth. Deposit ~3 um of Al over the storage-node contacts, seed pits with one imprint aligned to the contacts, and anodize at low voltage so the pores self-propagate straight down to AR >150:1; then line them with TiN/ZrO2/TiN by ALD.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and etch capex: no capacitor-hole mask and no high-AR mold etch; AR 150:1 at the same pitch gives ~2x Cs.

title: Catalytic metal-assisted etching drills 3D DRAM holes, no plasma
idea: First principle: plasma etch rate collapses with depth because ions and neutrals must reach the hole bottom (Knudsen transport), whereas metal-assisted chemical etching dissolves Si only at the catalyst/Si interface, so its rate does not depend on depth. Imprint Au or Pt nanodots on an epitaxial Si/SiGe superlattice and let them sink through 100+ tiers in HF/H2O2 to form the vertical bitline and channel holes of a 3D DRAM.
why: 3D DRAM blocker (fact 2) and etch capex: a wet bench replaces cryo-etch tools (~$5-8M each) and reaches tier counts where plasma etch stalls.

title: Vicinal-wafer atomic step bunches as litho-free wordline templates
idea: First principle: a Si wafer miscut by angle theta has atomic steps every a/tan(theta), and controlled step bunching during anneal forms periodic facets at a 10-30 nm pitch set only by theta and temperature. Decorate the bunched step edges by step-flow selective deposition (e.g., CaF2 or a silicide) to make parallel hard-mask lines across the whole wafer in one anneal, with zero lithography, for the wordline and bitline layers.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): line/space layers made with no mask and no scanner; pitch comes from crystallography instead of optics.

title: Dose-coded grayscale exposure defines three depths in one shot
idea: First principle: a mask carries 2D information, but exposure dose is a free third channel. A halftone grayscale reticle plus a resist with linear dose-to-depth contrast prints the buried-wordline trench, bitline-contact and isolation recess as three depth levels in one exposure, and a single etch with ~1:1 resist-to-substrate selectivity transfers all three.
why: Masks and steps (fact 4): 3 litho-etch modules become 1, saving ~2 critical masks and their overlay budget; ~5% lower wafer cost.

title: Run vertical gain-cell DRAM through idle 3D NAND fab lines
idea: First principle: most of the capital in a 3D NAND fab is alternating-stack deposition, high-AR channel-hole etch and staircase formation, which is exactly the tool set needed for a vertical-channel 2T0C gain cell: a stack of horizontal wordline layers pierced by oxide-semiconductor channels. Port the NAND flow (ONON stack, channel hole, replacement gate) to a gain-cell DRAM so NAND overcapacity in down-cycles produces DRAM with no new tools.
why: Capital intensity and time (facts 2, 4): reuses tens of $B of installed NAND capacity with no EUV; capacity in ~12 months instead of 3-5 years.

title: Grow capacitor electrodes upward by selective-area growth
idea: First principle: selective deposition happens only where surface chemistry allows, and unlike etch its rate does not depend on aspect ratio. Build the storage node bottom-up: selective-area MOCVD of conductive RuO2 or TiN nanopillars only on exposed storage-node contacts through a thin 100 nm template, braced by a lattice of nitride support rings, then wrap with high-k and a top plate.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and etch capex: removes the 1.5 um mold deposition, high-AR mold etch and mold strip; pillar height is limited by bracing, not by etch physics.

title: Defect-tolerant arrays delete half the in-line inspection tools
idea: First principle: yield is exp(-D0*Acrit), so 12% spare rows/columns plus per-subarray remap tables make yield insensitive to random defects up to ~5x today's D0. Spend that margin by skipping ~50% of optical and e-beam inspection and metrology steps (sample 1 wafer per lot) and relaxing some cleanroom zones from ISO 3 to ISO 5.
why: Capital and throughput: inspection/metrology is ~10-15% of fab tool capex and adds cycle time; ~8% capital saving for ~3% die-area overhead.

title: Area-selective deposition pattern propagation: zero-overlay layer stacking
idea: First principle: overlay error exists only because each layer is aligned optically; if each new layer nucleates only on a material exposed by the layer below (inhibitor SAMs that bind oxide but not metal, and the reverse), the pattern propagates chemically with zero misalignment. Design the cell so landing pads, contacts and the capacitor bottom electrode are each grown selectively on the previous layer, leaving one litho master for the array.
why: Litho and masks (fact 4): removes 2-3 critical masks and the overlay budget that limits 12 nm cells; tighter pitch without new optics.

title: Offset-cancelled sense amps shrink the capacitor to AR 20:1
idea: First principle: a cell must store only enough charge to beat the sense amp's offset, dV = (Vdd/2)*Cs/(Cs+Cbl) > ~3 sigma_offset. Put auto-zeroed, offset-cancelling sense amps under the array (bonded CMOS) and cut bitline length 4x so Cbl falls; then a ~1.5 fF cell built at AR ~20:1 with standard etch replaces the AR 70:1 pillar.
why: Capacitor wall and etch capex (facts 1, 4): removes the hardest high-AR etch and mold module; ~10-15% fewer process steps and higher yield.

title: Nanoimprint guides plus block-copolymer rectification replace EUV array layers
idea: First principle: imprint costs mechanical work, not photons (EUV turns ~0.02% of wall power into dose), but imprint suffers defects, while block copolymers anneal toward their free-energy minimum and heal defective guides. Imprint coarse 2x-pitch guides, then let a high-chi BCP (e.g., PS-b-PDMS) self-assemble to the final ~24 nm pitch, repairing imprint defects before pattern transfer.
why: EUV dependence (fact 4): tool ~$15M vs ~$200M and ~1/50 the power; removes the single-supplier EUV dependence for array layers.

title: Parallel MEMS tips write atom-precise imprint masters
idea: First principle: the resolution limit is one surface atom, which STM hydrogen-depassivation lithography reaches; it is slow, but a master only has to be written once. A 10,000-tip MEMS array writes a DRAM array master on H-terminated Si with ~1 nm edge roughness, selective ALD converts it to a hard template, and it is cloned into thousands of imprint working templates.
why: Mask cost and resolution (fact 4): masters with no stochastic edge roughness let imprint go below 10 nm half-pitch; master cost is spread over ~10^6 wafers.

title: BEOL-only oxide DRAM built in packaging-class back-end fabs
idea: First principle: channels only need high-temperature processing if they are single-crystal Si; amorphous oxide channels, ALD high-k and MIM capacitors all form below 400 C. Build the whole cell array (oxide-channel gain cells plus MIM capacitors) as back-end layers on cheap logic wafers in advanced-packaging/back-end fabs, which cost about 1/3 per wafer-pass of front-end fabs.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: runs on U.S. advanced-packaging lines being built under CHIPS, with no implanters, diffusion furnaces or EUV.

title: Purity only where electrons live: epi device layer on cheap substrate
idea: First principle: retention-critical leakage depends on defects within ~1 um of the surface, so 11N Czochralski purity in the other ~774 um is wasted. Grow a 3 um high-purity epitaxial device layer on substrates made from upgraded metallurgical-grade Si by directional solidification (no quartz CZ crucible), with a buried oxygen-precipitate getter to trap metals.
why: Scarce resources and cost: less dependence on Spruce Pine quartz crucibles and electronic-grade polysilicon; ~40-60% lower substrate cost.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling replaces helium in etch and deposition chucks
idea: First principle: helium is used under wafers only for heat transfer (0.15 W/m-K), and H2 conducts heat better (0.18 W/m-K) and can be made from water anywhere. Re-engineer electrostatic chucks to run 5-15 Torr pure-H2 backside gas with millimole-scale inventory, hydrogen sensors and catalytic recombiners on the chamber exhaust.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30%, offline since March 2026): removes one of the largest fab uses of helium and protects uptime from price spikes.

title: Solid-state 193 nm light sources remove neon and fluorine
idea: First principle: excimer gas is only a gain medium; 193 nm light can also come from frequency conversion of a ~1 um fiber laser through nonlinear crystals (harmonics plus sum-frequency mixing in CLBO/KBBF). Build a kW-class fiber-laser-pumped solid-state 193 nm source for immersion scanners with no neon/fluorine consumables, no gas-refill downtime and higher wall-plug efficiency.
why: Scarce resource (neon) and tool availability: higher DUV uptime makes DUV-heavy, EUV-free DRAM flows cheaper.

title: Continuous-flow inline fab: wafers stream under spatial process heads
idea: First principle: a DRAM wafer is actually being processed for only ~5% of its 60-90 day cycle; the rest is queueing between batch tools. Build array-module lines where single wafers ride gas bearings continuously under spatial ALD heads, spatial plasma etch heads and inline litho, like a printing press, cutting cycle time ~5x.
why: Capital and time: WIP inventory and idle tools are hidden capital; 3-5x faster learning cycles speed yield ramps.

title: Light-powered, contactless wafer-level DRAM test
idea: First principle: a retention test needs only power, a clock and a readout, and all three can be optical. Put a photodiode power island and a micro-LED or optical modulator on each die, flood-light the whole wafer so every die runs BIST march and retention tests in parallel, and read pass/fail maps with a camera, replacing probe cards and most testers.
why: Test capital and throughput: DRAM testers and probe cards are billions of dollars of capex; full-wafer parallel test in minutes.

title: Deep trench capacitors etched into the thinned wafer backside
idea: First principle: frontside capacitors compete for height inside a ~2 um back-end stack, while the substrate below the transistor is idle volume. After frontside transistors are made and bonded to a carrier, thin the wafer to ~1.5 um and etch single-crystal Si trenches (AR ~40, which etches more uniformly than oxide/nitride molds) from the backside, aligned to the storage nodes with backside-power-delivery alignment tools.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): decouples the capacitor from frontside wiring and reuses the BSPDN tooling now being installed for logic.

title: Periphery from depreciated U.S. logic fabs, hybrid-bonded to array
idea: First principle: the array needs the finest pitch, but the periphery (~49% of the die) only needs ~28 nm-class CMOS. Make array-only wafers in the DRAM fab and the periphery on fully depreciated 28-65 nm U.S. logic fabs, then join them by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and capital: up to ~1.8x bits per expensive DRAM wafer, using idle U.S. mature-node capacity.

title: MLCC-style laminated capacitor: deposit plates, don't etch towers
idea: First principle: capacitance needs electrode area, which can come from many thin horizontal plates, as in a multilayer ceramic capacitor, instead of one tall vertical tower. Deposit 30 alternating TiN/high-k layers as blankets, punch one shallow hole per cell, and use selective lateral recess plus side contacts to tie odd plates to the storage node and even plates to the plate line.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): area comes from the number of depositions, which is cheap and AR-free; 5+ fF with hole AR <20:1.

title: One ALD chemistry family builds every layer of the cell
idea: First principle: tool count scales with the number of distinct materials in the flow. Make the channel (IGZO), electrodes (degenerate In2O3:H/ITO), dielectric (Ga2O3/HfO2 laminate) and passivation from one In/Ga/Zn/Hf precursor set in one multi-station ALD cluster, changing only cycle ratios and oxidant.
why: Capital and tool set: ~5 tool types collapse into one platform, with a simpler U.S. tool supply chain.

title: Four bonded DUV array tiers beat one EUV tier on density
idea: First principle: cost per bit = wafer cost / bits. A fully depreciated, DUV-only 16 nm-class 6F2 array wafer gives ~56% of the bits of a 12 nm EUV wafer at roughly half its cost, and face-to-back hybrid bonding of four such array tiers onto one periphery wafer, linked by ~1 um inter-tier vias, gives ~2.2x bits per footprint.
why: EUV dependence and capital (fact 4): cost per bit at parity to ~10% lower with zero EUV, about 2x density per package footprint, all on installed tools.

title: Exfoliate device layers, reuse the donor wafer fifty times
idea: First principle: a DRAM device needs about 1 um of single-crystal Si, so 99.9% of a 775 um wafer is just a mechanical carrier. Transfer 1 um device layers by hydrogen-implant cleaving or controlled spalling from a premium donor onto handles made of recycled Si, then re-polish and reuse the donor 30-50 times.
why: Scarce resources (quartz crucibles, polysilicon) and cost: up to ~30x less CZ crystal per wafer; the substrate is recycled by design.

title: Cold-crucible Czochralski: silicon contains itself, no quartz consumed
idea: First principle: the quartz crucible is consumed only because it touches molten Si at 1414 C, but molten Si can sit in a thin frozen skin of its own Si inside a segmented, water-cooled copper crucible heated by induction. Grow DRAM-grade crystals by skull-melting CZ; the copper crucible is repaired and reused indefinitely, and the skull is remelted into the next charge.
why: Spruce Pine (>80%) quartz-crucible chokepoint: removes the consumable, and less oxygen dissolves into the crystal.

title: Rework-orthogonal layer stack: strip and redo any failed step
idea: First principle: wafers are scrapped because removing a bad layer damages the layers beneath. Give each pair of adjacent layers an etchant with >1000:1 selectivity (for example, thin Ge-rich sacrificial interlayers under metals that dissolve in H2O2), so any misprocessed module can be stripped and redeposited, extending rework loops from litho to every module.
why: Capital per good wafer: 2-5% line-yield loss on ~$15k wafers becomes rework; the flow is repairable by design.

title: Debondable hybrid-bond layer lets you swap the bad HBM tier
idea: First principle: stack yield falls as y^n because one bad die kills the stack; if the bond is reversible, a failure costs one die instead. Bond Cu pads through a thin indium or Sn-Bi interlayer, with a dielectric that softens near 200 C, so a stack with one failed die is locally reheated, split and rebonded with a known-good die.
why: HBM yield tax (fact 6, 20-30% lost): recovers most failed stacks; ~20% lower capital per good bit.

title: Liquid-metal microbumps make memory stacks hot-swappable
idea: First principle: solder joints are permanent because they solidify, while gallium-indium-tin eutectic stays liquid above ~11 C and wets only treated pads. Connect DRAM dies to a base die through Galinstan-filled micro-wells sealed by a polymer gasket and held by a mechanical clamp, so dies can be pulled, tested and replaced at room temperature.
why: Repairability and yield: known-good stacks after assembly and die reuse at end of life, with no reflow damage.

title: Spare-tier HBM: thirteen dies for twelve, fused at test
idea: First principle: with die yield y = 0.98, a 12-high stack yields 0.98^12 = ~79%, but one spare die plus a TSV crossbar remap programmed by e-fuse after stack test gives P(at most 1 failure in 13) = ~97%. Add one redundant die per stack and steer around any bad die at test, and again in the field.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): 21% stack loss becomes ~3% for 8% extra silicon; repairable by design.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM with fault-mapped mesh; no dicing or packages
idea: First principle: dicing, packaging and final test are ~15-25% of DRAM cost, and a wafer can stay one device if defects are routed around. Keep the 300 mm wafer as one memory with a reconfigurable on-wafer mesh network and per-tile power gates, so defective or worn tiles are mapped out at test and in the field, and the wafer goes back for tile-level reclaim.
why: Cost per bit and capital (packaging, test, TSVs): ~2 TB per wafer as one repairable unit.

title: Reverse fab: harvest, retest and rebin retired server DRAM
idea: First principle: DRAM has effectively unlimited endurance and no dominant wear-out, so a 5-year-old die is physically almost as good as new. Build automated lines that desolder DRAM packages from retired DIMMs and boards, reball them, run full BIST, retention and row-hammer binning, and assemble certified second-life modules.
why: Supply: hyperscalers retire many exabytes of DRAM per year; recovered bits cost ~5% of new-fab capex per bit and arrive in months.

title: Lease bit-hours with guaranteed take-back of every module
idea: First principle: memory's value is the service (bit-hours), not ownership, and ownership strands bits in idle or retired machines. Sell DRAM as a lease priced per GB-month with contractual take-back, embedded serial and health logs, and redeployment of returned modules into lower-tier fleets.
why: Usable supply: ~1.5-2x more lifetime use per fabricated bit; recurring revenue finances fabs.

title: Thermoplastic, solvent-release packages make DRAM dies recoverable
idea: First principle: epoxy molding compound is a thermoset that cannot be undone, so it traps the die forever. Package DRAM in a high-Tg thermoplastic (e.g., liquid-crystal polymer) with a solvent-releasable underfill, so a low-temperature solvent bath frees bare, intact dies for retest and redeployment.
why: Recyclability: die-level reuse plus gold/copper recovery; feeds reverse-fab supply.

title: Self-unzipping resists recovered as monomer and repolymerized
idea: First principle: lithography needs only a transient chemical contrast, yet resist is burned or dumped. Use low-ceiling-temperature polymers (e.g., polyphthalaldehyde) that depolymerize fully to monomer under exposure or mild heat, capture the evaporated monomer in a cold trap on the track, then purify and repolymerize it.
why: Consumables and steps: removes solvent strip steps and resist waste; dry development also avoids pattern collapse.

title: Reusable capacitor-forest template: grow once, transfer-print many times
idea: First principle: the costly high-AR etch only defines a shape, and a shape can be reused if the mold separates cleanly. Etch one master Si template with high-AR pores, grow capacitor electrodes plus high-k inside a release liner, transfer-bond the capacitor forest onto the storage-node contacts, and lift the template off for 50-100 reuses.
why: Capacitor etch capex (fact 1): the hardest etch is amortized over many wafers; the template is reused by design.

title: Regenerable release coating extends imprint template life tenfold
idea: First principle: template wear happens in the top few nm where contact occurs, so the template body never needs replacing if its surface can be renewed. Coat imprint templates with a ~2 nm ALD sacrificial layer (Al2O3 plus fluorinated SAM) that is stripped and redeposited every ~1,000 imprints to restore the exact CD.
why: Mask/template cost for EUV-free imprint (fact 4): ~10x lower template cost per wafer.

title: Fab-scale noble-gas fractionation recovers helium, neon and xenon
idea: First principle: helium, neon, krypton and xenon are chemically inert, so consuming them is a design choice. Route every tool exhaust to a fab-level cryogenic separation and membrane plant that recovers >90% of the noble gases and reinjects purified gas, with tools standardized to closed-loop gas ports.
why: Helium chokepoint and neon risk: 80-90% less purchased He; protects uptime and price.

title: Electrochemically regenerated wet chemistry: etchants as closed loops
idea: First principle: in most cleans the oxidant is consumed but the acid matrix is not. Regenerate sulfuric-peroxide (SPM) on site as electrochemical persulfate, recover HF/HNO3 by membrane distillation, and electrowin dissolved metals, so wet benches run closed-loop.
why: Water, chemicals and opex: ~70% less chemical purchase and much less UPW; eases U.S. permitting.

title: Open-standard modular fab tools with swappable chambers
idea: First principle: a process tool is a vacuum chamber plus a few energy and gas sources, and most of its price is integration, not physics. Define an open mechanical, electrical and software chamber standard so U.S. vendors build interchangeable process modules that are repaired, upgraded and redeployed on common transfer platforms over 25-year lives.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: lower tool cost, longer asset life, less vendor lock-in.

title: Relocatable fab pods: containerized modules with high resale value
idea: First principle: fab capital is expensive partly because it is stranded: a fab building cannot be moved or resold. Factory-build fab segments as sealed clean pods with minienvironment tools inside, bolt them together in months, and move, refurbish or resell them later, which lowers the risk premium on capital.
why: Capital intensity and time to capacity (3-5 years today): ~12-18 month deployment; redeployable by design.

title: Electrorefine wafering kerf back into crystal feedstock
idea: First principle: diamond-wire slicing turns ~100-150 um of 11N Si per cut into sludge, yet the Si atoms are still pure. Collect the kerf, separate abrasive and coolant, strip the surface oxide, and electrorefine and remelt it into polysilicon feedstock for the next boule.
why: Scarce resource and polysilicon cost: recovers ~15-25% of crystal mass now lost per wafer; recycled by design.

title: Self-healing capacitor dielectric via in-field oxygen-vacancy anneal
idea: First principle: high-k leakage tails come from mobile oxygen-vacancy clusters, which field and heat can redistribute. Add an array-level reverse-bias plus on-die microheater pulse (~300 C for microseconds) during idle that disperses vacancy clusters in ZrO2/HfO2, repairing weak cells in the field so the fab can relax its leakage-tail screen.
why: Leakage tail and yield (fact 3): fewer weak bits scrapped or fused out; longer refresh intervals.

title: Capture and regenerate the 95% of ALD precursor that misses wafers
idea: First principle: ALD uses one monolayer per cycle, so ~95-99% of Hf, Zr and Ru precursor flows to the exhaust or the chamber walls. Fit each ALD exhaust with a cold-trap or sorbent cartridge that captures unreacted metal-organic precursor, and return the cartridges to the precursor maker to be regenerated into fresh precursor.
why: Scarce-resource intensity (Hf, Ru) and opex: ~5x less precursor purchased; recycled by design.

title: Re-patternable EUV mask blanks: strip absorber, keep the multilayer
idea: First principle: an EUV mask's value is its defect-free Mo/Si multilayer blank, and the pattern is just information in the absorber. Add an etch-stop capping layer so the absorber can be stripped without damaging the blank, and rewrite the same blank with a new pattern when a design is revised.
why: Mask cost (fact 4): the blank is a large share of EUV reticle cost, so reuse cuts mask spend ~40%.

title: Laser-CVD wafer repair of interconnect opens, borrowed from displays
idea: First principle: an open in an upper metal line is just ~10^9 missing atoms, which laser-induced chemical vapor deposition can add precisely, as LCD panel lines are repaired today. After wafer probe, locate opens and shorts in the top metal and redistribution layers, then write or cut them at laser-CVD and ablation stations.
why: Yield and capital per good die: part of the yield loss becomes repair; repairable by design.

title: Open repair-port mandate lets anyone rebin and repair DRAM
idea: First principle: every DRAM already holds spare rows and post-package-repair fuses; only the access is closed. Create a JEDEC standard and a procurement rule requiring a documented, authenticated repair interface (PPR, fuse map, test modes) on all DRAM, so third parties can repair and rebin used and marginal parts.
why: Usable supply: part of discarded and marginal DRAM becomes usable stock; enables reverse-fab businesses.
